title: Account Manipulation: Additional Local or Domain Groups
shortTitle: Account Manipulation: Additional Local or Domain Groups
summary: This sub-technique of account manipulation is the plain group membership change: adding an account the adversary controls to a local group or a directory group that carries extra rights. On Windows this is usually done with the built-in net commands for local and domain groups, and on Linux with the user modification command that edits group membership. The classic targets are the local administrators group, which gives lasting elevated rights on a device, and the remote desktop users group, which allows a future interactive logon to that endpoint. Adding an account to a virtual private network user group creates persistence at the network edge rather than on a single host, and adding a Linux account to the administrative group lets it use elevated commands through the sudo feature. In Windows domains, machine accounts can also be added to domain groups, which lets the local system account hold rights in the directory. Detection combines directory and host logs: group membership change events on the server side, process creation records showing the group modification commands on the endpoint, and subsequent logon events from the newly privileged account.

beginner.definition: This is a sub-technique of account manipulation. It means an attacker adds an account to a group that has more rights than the account should have. A group is a container of accounts that all share the same permissions. Joining the right group is often all it takes to become an administrator.
beginner.whyItMatters: Group membership is the easiest way to keep power on a system. It survives a password change, because the account still belongs to the group. It also looks tidy and intentional in the user list, so nobody notices anything broken. Left unchecked, an added account can return weeks later with full rights.
howItWorks: The attacker gets an account or administrator access that can change group membership.
They add an account they control to the local administrators group on a device.
They may also add it to the remote desktop users group so they can log in later.
On Linux they add the account to the administrative group that may use elevated commands.
Adding an account to a virtual private network group gives access to the network itself.
In a Windows domain, machine accounts can be added to domain groups for wider rights.
beginner.example: Think of a residents committee where only committee members may open the storage room. Someone adds a neighbour's name to the committee list at the front desk. No lock is broken and no key is copied. The neighbour simply signs the list, and every door that trusts that list opens for them.
takeaways: Track who joins powerful groups such as administrators and remote desktop users.
Review group membership as often as you review accounts and passwords.
Look for the group change command itself in process logs, not only the result.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent account manipulation technique.
Describe the behaviours it covers, including local group, domain group and network group changes.
Identify the group membership change events and command records that reveal it.
Distinguish legitimate group administration from adversary membership addition.
Explain how group membership provides lasting privilege without any exploit.
